title: Life Assurance Underwriting: Principles and Best Practices

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Define underwriting in the context of life assurance and explain the concept of anti-selection, including why its management is fundamental to the financial stability of a life insurance risk pool.

Identify and assess the principal individual risk factors considered in life assurance underwriting (age, sex, health, occupation, lifestyle, family history, financial status, and geographic location) and explain how each influences the underwriting decision.

Describe the structure of medical evidence requirements in life underwriting, including non-medical limits, the circumstances requiring medical examination, the Attending Physician Statement, and special pathology investigations.
Explain the range of special terms available to the underwriter (exclusions, flat extra premiums, percentage loadings, postponements, and declinatures) and the criteria governing their application.
Define moratorium underwriting and explain its application in Nigerian group and bancassurance business.
Apply an occupational hazard classification framework and explain how occupational risk loadings are calculated and applied.
Explain the underwriting approach to three special risk categories (aviation, drug use, and HIV/AIDS) with specific reference to NIIRA 2025 obligations regarding HIV non-discrimination.

Describe the principles of financial underwriting, including insurable interest, income multiples, over-insurance assessment, and the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) obligations that arise in the underwriting process.

Describe NIIRA 2025’s requirements for actuarial oversight of underwriting practices, including the statutory actuary’s responsibilities in relation to non-medical limits, reinsurance treaties, and underwriting adequacy.

Explain best-practice underwriting operations including triage models, digital-first evidence gathering, turnaround time KPIs, consistency frameworks, and structured underwriter competency development.

blocks.text: 11.1 Introduction: The Purpose and Discipline of Underwriting

blocks.h: Underwriting is the act of individual risk selection and classification by which a life insurer determines whether to accept a proposed life assured for coverage and, if so, on what terms and at what premium. It is the commercial mechanism through which the insurer maintains the integrity of the risk pool on which its pricing and reserving assumptions are based.

The economic justification for underwriting rests on the concept of anti-selection (also called adverse selection). Left unchecked, individuals with impaired health, hazardous occupations, or elevated mortality risk are more likely to seek life insurance, and more likely to purchase larger amounts of it, than healthy individuals. If insurers accepted all proposals at standard premium rates without differentiation, the actual claims experience of the portfolio would be materially worse than the population average assumed in pricing, and the product would become unprofitable. Underwriting is, at its most fundamental level, a defence against the systematic overrepresentation of high-risk lives in the insured pool.

This defence must, however, be exercised with proportionality and, increasingly, with legal compliance. The principle of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) (which requires the proposer to disclose all material facts affecting the insurer’s assessment of the risk) creates a bilateral obligation: the insurer must disclose its assessment criteria in its proposal forms and must apply them consistently and fairly. In Nigeria, NIIRA 2025 imposes explicit non-discrimination obligations in respect of HIV/AIDS status, and the National Data Protection Act 2023 governs the collection and processing of health data in the underwriting process. Underwriting is therefore both a financial function and a consumer-facing compliance function.

The Nigerian underwriting environment presents specific challenges not present in more mature markets. Mortality data quality is limited: the EFU Life Table, while the standard actuarial reference, was developed from the experience of a relatively small insured population and may not fully capture mortality patterns in rural, northern, or low-income urban segments. Health infrastructure is uneven: medical examination facilities and the quality of Attending Physician Statements vary significantly across the country. Anti-selection risk is amplified by low general insurance literacy, policyholders may not appreciate the duty of disclosure, leading to unintentional non-disclosure that creates claims disputes.

Against this backdrop, life insurers operating in Nigeria must build underwriting operations that are technically rigorous, operationally efficient, legally compliant, and commercially intelligent, capable of offering standard terms to the widest possible market while protecting the risk pool from material anti-selection.

The underwriting process begins when a completed proposal form (or its digital equivalent) is received from the distribution channel and ends with the issue of a policy on defined terms or a formal declination. Between these two points, the underwriter collects and evaluates risk information, consults internal guidelines and reinsurer treaties, seeks additional medical or financial evidence where required, and arrives at a decision consistent with the company’s underwriting philosophy and commercial objectives.

blocks.title: Process: The Individual Life Underwriting Sequence, Seven Steps

blocks.h: Step 1: Proposal Receipt and Completeness Check. The proposal form is received (on paper, via agent, or digitally). The underwriting team checks that all required fields are completed, that the applicant’s signature is present, and that required supporting documents (birth certificate, identification) accompany the proposal. Incomplete proposals are returned for completion before further assessment begins.

Step 2: Financial Assessment. The underwriter verifies that the proposed sum assured is proportionate to the applicant’s declared income and financial status. Financial underwriting limits and income multiples are applied (see Section 11.8). AML/KYC checks are completed.

Step 3: Non-Medical Assessment. The underwriter reviews the applicant’s age, sex, occupation, lifestyle disclosures, family history, and health declarations against the company’s non-medical underwriting guidelines. If the proposed sum assured is below the Non-Medical Limit (NML) and the health declarations are clear, the policy may be issued at standard terms without medical examination.

Step 4: Medical Evidence Gathering (if required). Where the proposed sum assured exceeds the NML, or where the health declarations disclose a condition requiring further investigation, the underwriter requests the required medical evidence: GP examination, specialist report, Attending Physician Statement, blood tests, or other investigations.

Step 5: Risk Assessment and Classification. The underwriter evaluates all available information against the company’s underwriting manual, reinsurer guidelines, and the statutory actuary’s directives. The risk is classified as: standard (issue at normal rates); impaired (issue with special terms); or unacceptable (postpone or decline).

Step 6: Reinsurance Referral (if required). Proposals exceeding the company’s automatic treaty retention limit, or involving unusual or complex medical risks, are referred to the reinsurer for a facultative underwriting opinion (see Section 11.10).

Step 7: Decision Communication and Policy Issue. The underwriting decision (standard acceptance, modified acceptance [with special terms], postponement, or declination) is communicated to the applicant through the distribution channel. Policies accepted on standard or modified terms are issued. Declined proposals are communicated with the reasons required by NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions.

Life assurance underwriting decisions exist on a spectrum from unconditional standard acceptance to outright declination. Between these poles, underwriters have a range of tools to accommodate impaired risks while preserving the technical integrity of the premium rate charged.

rows: Policy issued on standard terms at the filed premium rate without modification.
All risk factors within normal limits; no material health impairment; sum assured within NML or medical evidence satisfactory.
Policy issued at standard premium, but with a clause excluding claims arising from a specific named condition.
Pre-existing condition that is well-defined and compartmentalised (e.g., existing back condition, named mental health diagnosis).
A fixed additional annual premium (per ₦1,000 sum assured) is charged, typically for a defined period.
Impairments with time-limited excess mortality (post-surgery recovery, treated malignancy in remission).
The standard premium is increased by a defined percentage (e.g., 50%, 100%, 200%).
Impairments with a proportionate, sustained excess mortality, controlled hypertension, elevated BMI, moderate occupational hazard.
Policy accepted but at a lower sum assured than applied for.
Used where the financial underwriting assessment does not support the full applied amount.
Application suspended; reapplication invited after a defined period or event.
Recovering from surgery, recent significant illness, current investigations pending, recent bereavement.
Uninsurable risk: terminal illness, recent major medical event, extreme occupational hazard with no reinsurer support.

blocks.h: Different distribution channels generate business with different risk profiles, and underwriting procedures must be calibrated accordingly. Most life insurance companies operate a tiered delegation authority: field underwriters (or agents with limited underwriting authority) may issue policies up to a defined NML limit; branch underwriters handle cases up to a higher limit or involving specified disclosures; head office underwriters deal with complex or large cases; and the Chief Underwriting Officer or a specialist panel reviews exceptional referrals.

In the Nigerian context, the digital and bancassurance channels present particular delegation challenges. Embedding simplified underwriting into a USSD or mobile application, or processing credit life proposals at bank branch level, requires carefully designed decision rules, typically simple yes/no health declarations with automatic acceptance below a defined sum assured limit and escalation for anything above. The design of these embedded underwriting rules is a joint responsibility of the actuarial, underwriting, and technology functions.

blocks.text: 11.3 Individual Risk Factors in Life Assurance Underwriting

blocks.h: The underwriter’s fundamental task is to assess the degree to which a proposed life assured’s mortality risk deviates from the average mortality of the population on which the standard premium has been calculated. This deviation is assessed by reference to a set of individual risk factors. The principal risk factors assessed in individual life underwriting are: age and sex, current health and medical history, occupation, lifestyle, family history, financial status, and geographic location.

Age is the single most powerful predictor of mortality risk in life assurance underwriting. The probability of death in any given year (qx) increases with age, a feature embedded in all standard mortality tables. Because premium rates are age-banded, the age at entry determines the rate schedule applicable to the policy. In Nigeria, accurate age verification is an underwriting requirement: the EFU Life Table’s qx values are directly keyed to exact age, and a year’s error in recorded age can materially mis-price the risk. Accepted age evidence includes national identity card, birth certificate, international passport, and voter’s card.

Sex is a significant mortality differentiator. Female mortality rates (qx) are lower than male rates at virtually all ages in the EFU Life Table, a pattern consistent with global actuarial experience. Standard practice in Nigerian life underwriting is to use sex-differentiated premium rates. Products that use unisex rates (common in some microinsurance products for administrative simplicity) implicitly cross-subsidise male risks from female policyholders, a feature that must be reflected in the pricing assumption.

The proposer’s current health status and medical history are assessed primarily through the declaration section of the proposal form. The standard Nigerian proposal form invites disclosure of: current and recent illnesses; previous hospitalisation or surgery; ongoing medication; diagnosed chronic conditions (hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, asthma, cancer, HIV/AIDS, kidney disease, epilepsy); and any conditions for which medical advice or treatment has been sought in the preceding five to ten years.
Common impairments encountered in Nigerian individual life underwriting, and their typical underwriting treatment, include:

rows: Standard or small loading (25–50%) depending on control and target organ damage.
Loading 50–150%; exclusion of cerebrovascular/cardiovascular complications if uncontrolled.
Loading 50–150%; evidence of recent HbA1c, BP, and renal function required.
Type 2 diabetes (poorly controlled or with complications)
Loading 100–300% or declination depending on severity.
Under NIIRA 2025: no declination solely on HIV status; loading based on CD4 count and viral load evidence. See Section 11.7.3.
Flat extra for defined period post-remission; some cancers fully loadable after 5-year remission.
Postpone if recent; after confirmed cure, loadings typically 50–100% or standard after extended remission.
Build tables used; loadings from 25% upward depending on degree of obesity and co-morbidities.
Loading 75–150%; exclusion for accidental death under certain circumstances.
Decline in early post-operative period; loadings 100–300% after recovery period.
Significant loading or declination depending on clinical history and severity.

blocks.h: A proposer’s occupation affects life assurance risk in two ways: physical hazard (the direct risk of death or injury from the nature of the work) and moral hazard (the risk that the insured will not exercise appropriate care or may take undue risks because of the existence of insurance). Physical occupational hazard is the more quantifiable of the two and is the primary driver of occupational underwriting decisions.

Detailed occupational hazard classification is addressed in Section 11.6. For the purpose of the initial risk assessment, the underwriter identifies whether the proposed life assured works in an occupation associated with higher-than-average physical risk and, if so, refers to the company’s occupational hazard schedule or reinsurer guidelines for the appropriate underwriting action.

Smoking. Smokers carry a materially higher mortality risk than non-smokers across all age bands. Standard underwriting practice globally is to charge smoker rates, which typically range from 25% to 100% above non-smoker rates depending on age and product type. In the Nigerian market, cigar, pipe, and other tobacco use is treated on the same basis as cigarette smoking. Where a proposer discloses they are a former smoker, most Nigerian insurers apply non-smoker rates after a defined cessation period (commonly 12 months, some requiring 24 months).

Alcohol use. Moderate alcohol use does not attract additional loading. Heavy or hazardous drinking (defined by clinical indicators, elevated liver enzymes, history of alcohol-related illness, stated weekly consumption significantly above safe limits) attracts loadings or exclusions depending on severity. Alcoholism or alcohol dependency is typically declined.

Dangerous hobbies and activities. Recreational activities that create material excess mortality risk are assessed separately from occupation. In the Nigerian context, relevant activities include amateur aviation, offshore sea fishing, motor racing, mountaineering, and combat sports. The underwriting action ranges from a flat extra premium (for activities with quantifiable excess risk) to exclusion of claims arising from the specific activity.
Drug use. Addressed separately in Section 11.7.2 due to the specific complexity of the risk assessment.

Family history is relevant where there is evidence of hereditary conditions with a material impact on life expectancy. Conditions of significance in life assurance underwriting include: early-onset cardiovascular disease (father or male first-degree relative dying of heart attack before age 60; mother or female first-degree relative before age 65); hereditary cancers (familial adenomatous polyposis, BRCA1/2 mutations if disclosed, familial melanoma); polycystic kidney disease; Huntington’s disease; and hereditary hypercholesterolaemia.

In practice, Nigerian underwriters apply family history loadings with caution. Mortality data on hereditary conditions in the Nigerian population is limited, and the reliability of family history disclosure is variable. Standard practice is to note the family history and apply a modest loading (typically 25–50%) where there is strong evidence of heritable excess risk, while reserving heavier loadings for cases where the proposer’s own health investigations suggest early signs of the hereditary condition.

The proposer’s financial status is relevant to underwriting for two reasons: it determines the appropriate level of insurable interest (see Section 11.8.2), and it provides evidence relevant to the assessment of moral hazard. A proposal for a sum assured that is grossly disproportionate to the proposer’s declared income may indicate over-insurance, which creates a financial incentive for fraud. Financial underwriting is therefore an integral component of the risk assessment process, not a separate administrative step.

Financial underwriting uses income multiples to set maximum sum assured limits by income band. Typical Nigerian market practice, aligned with reinsurer guidelines, uses multiples in the range of 10 to 20 times annual income for individuals under 40, declining to 5 to 10 times annual income for individuals approaching retirement age. The rationale is that insurance is a mechanism for replacing lost income, not for generating a windfall.

Geographic location is a relevant underwriting factor in the Nigerian context due to the material differences in mortality risk, healthcare access, and political/security risk across the country’s 36 states. Factors that underwriters consider include:

items.h: Access to healthcare: residents of rural areas with limited access to tertiary medical facilities have materially worse outcomes from treatable conditions (cardiovascular events, diabetes complications, cancer) than urban residents.

Security environment: some parts of the country have experienced elevated mortality from civil conflict, banditry, or terrorism. Underwriters writing individual policies for residents of high-risk security zones may apply loadings or specific exclusions for violent death.
Environmental health: exposure to industrial pollution, contaminated water sources, or communicable disease environments specific to certain geographies.
Occupational geography: certain geographic concentrations of high-risk occupations (offshore oil and gas workers, mining communities) require specific underwriting treatment.

blocks.h: Nigerian insurers typically use a regional zone framework (Lagos/South West; South East; South South/Niger Delta; North West; North East; North Central) with specific underwriting guidance or loadings for zones assessed as materially higher risk. These frameworks are usually confidential commercial documents and form part of the underwriting manual.

A Non-Medical Limit (NML) is the maximum sum assured up to which the insurer is prepared to accept a life on the basis of the proposal form declarations alone, without requiring a medical examination. Below the NML, the underwriter relies on: the proposer’s responses to the health declaration questions on the proposal form; the proposer’s age; and any additional financial underwriting checks. Above the NML, a medical examination is automatically required.

The NML is set by the actuary in consultation with the Chief Underwriting Officer and the reinsurer, based on the company’s reinsurance treaty terms (reinsurers often specify minimum NML requirements as a condition of their treaties) and on the statistical relationship between proposal form declarations and actual claims experience. A higher NML means faster processing and lower distribution friction; a lower NML provides greater medical evidence on larger risks. The trade-off is between administrative efficiency and risk control.

rows: Youngest age band; low baseline mortality; high reliance on health declarations.
Elevated chronic disease incidence; NML reduced.
Significant increase in cardiovascular and metabolic conditions; medical examination more critical.
High mortality risk age band; medical examination expected for all but smallest sums assured.

blocks.h: Note: The above are indicative of market practice. Individual insurers’ NMLs vary based on their portfolio profile, reinsurance treaty requirements, and risk appetite. NMLs are typically higher for group life business due to the averaging effect of the group.

Where a medical examination is required (either because the proposed sum assured exceeds the NML or because the health declarations indicate a condition requiring clinical verification) the underwriter specifies the type and scope of examination required. The insurer bears the cost of medically required examinations for proposals it has invited.

Medical examinations in Nigerian life underwriting are conducted by approved medical examiners, registered medical practitioners on the insurer’s approved panel. Panel management is a significant operational function: maintaining a geographically spread panel of competent examiners who use standardised examination forms and report reliably is a material challenge for insurers operating across Nigeria’s 36 states. The use of tele-medicine platforms and video consultation by approved examiners is an emerging practice that is reducing geographic barriers to medical evidence collection.
Standard examination requirements by sum assured band are as follows:

rows: Basic GP examination: height, weight, blood pressure, urinalysis, ECG (age 40+). Health declaration verification.
Full GP examination + resting ECG + full blood count + biochemistry profile (renal, liver function, fasting glucose, cholesterol).
Above + HIV/HBsAg serology + chest X-ray (age 45+) + specialist report if any declaration.
Above + stress ECG (age 40+) + echocardiogram (age 50+) + reinsurer review. Additional investigations as indicated by clinical findings.

blocks.h: An Attending Physician Statement (APS), also called a General Practitioner’s Report or Confidential Medical Report, is a structured report completed by the proposer’s own treating doctor or specialist at the insurer’s request, following the proposer’s signed consent. It provides a professional third-party account of the medical history, current status, and prognosis of a condition disclosed in the proposal form.

The APS is the most clinically informative of the standard medical evidence tools available to the underwriter. A well-completed APS from an experienced clinician familiar with the proposer’s history provides diagnostic precision that the medical examination alone cannot. Its limitations are: availability (many Nigerians lack a registered GP with comprehensive records, particularly in informal urban and rural settings); cost and turnaround time; and the variable quality of APS completion, which requires ongoing quality management by the underwriting function.

Key information an APS should provide: diagnosis and date of diagnosis; treatment history and current medication; most recent objective clinical measurements (blood pressure, HbA1c, CD4 count as relevant); compliance with treatment; history of hospitalisation; prognosis and medical opinion on life expectancy; and the physician’s recommendation on insurability.

Beyond the standard blood and urine tests included in the medical examination requirement, the underwriter may request specialist investigations for specific risk factors. Common special investigations in Nigerian life underwriting include:

items.h: HIV serology (ELISA + Western Blot confirmation): Required above defined sum assured limits and where relevant to the health declaration. NIIRA 2025 obligations on HIV underwriting are addressed in Section 11.7.3.
HBsAg and HCV serology: Hepatitis B and C are prevalent in Nigeria; positive serology with evidence of chronic active disease attracts significant loadings or declination.
Echocardiogram: Required for large sum assureds at older ages and where there is a history of cardiac symptoms or ECG abnormalities.
Chest X-ray: Required for respiratory disclosures, history of tuberculosis, or smokers above defined age thresholds.
HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin): Essential for diabetes assessment; provides a three-month blood glucose average more reliable than a single fasting glucose reading.
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA): For male proposers above age 50 at higher sum assured levels.
Sickle cell electrophoresis: Relevant to the Nigerian genetic disease context; full assessment required for HbSS and HbSC variants.

blocks.text: 11.5 Special Terms and Adverse Underwriting Decisions

blocks.h: An exclusion is a contractual clause that limits the insurer’s liability by excluding claims arising from a specified cause or condition. Exclusions are used where the proposer has a known condition that creates an identifiable, compartmentalised excess mortality risk that cannot be fairly priced through a loading, but where the individual is otherwise insurable.

Exclusions must be clearly worded, specifically defined, communicated in writing to the proposer before the policy is issued, and acknowledged by the proposer’s signed endorsement. An exclusion that has not been properly disclosed to and acknowledged by the proposer may be unenforceable under NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions.

Common life assurance exclusions in the Nigerian market: death resulting from the progression of a named pre-existing condition; accidental death arising from participation in a named dangerous activity; death from certain specified medical procedures known to carry elevated operative risk.

Where the underwriter assesses that the proposed life assured carries excess mortality risk that is proportionate and persistent over time, the appropriate response is a premium loading rather than an exclusion. Loadings are of two types:

Percentage extra (or multiplicative loading): The standard premium is multiplied by a factor greater than 1. A policy with a standard premium of ₦50,000 at a 150% loading would be issued at ₦75,000. Percentage extras are appropriate where the excess mortality risk is proportionate to the base risk at each age, for instance, where the impairment causes a consistent percentage increase in qx across the policy term.

Flat extra (or additive loading): A fixed additional premium per ₦1,000 sum assured per year is charged on top of the standard premium. A flat extra of ₦5 per ₦1,000 sum assured on a ₦10,000,000 policy amounts to an additional ₦50,000 per year. Flat extras are appropriate where the excess mortality risk is relatively constant rather than increasing with age, for instance, for occupational hazards or for conditions in early post-treatment remission.

Flat extras are typically applied for a defined period. As the underlying condition improves or the occupational exposure changes, the flat extra may be reviewed and removed. Most Nigerian insurers’ underwriting manuals specify standard flat extra amounts for common impairments, derived from reinsurer data and international actuarial sources such as the Munich Re underwriting manual or Swiss Re’s Life Guide.

A postponement is a temporary suspension of the proposal. The insurer declines to issue the policy at the time of application but invites the proposer to reapply after a defined condition is met: a period of treatment, a post-surgical recovery period, the completion of specialist investigations, or the passage of a defined duration from a significant health event.

Postponement is different from declination: it implies that the risk is not permanently uninsurable but is currently unassessable or temporarily elevated. Common grounds for postponement in Nigerian practice include: recent cardiac event (reapply 6–12 months post-event); pending hospital investigations for an undiagnosed condition; recent surgery in recovery; severe obesity where weight-reduction programme is under way; recent diagnosis of a condition not yet stabilised by treatment.
The period of postponement should be communicated clearly to the proposer, together with the evidence that will be required when they reapply.

A declination is a final decision by the insurer not to offer insurance to the proposer on any terms. Declinations arise where the mortality risk is so severely elevated that no premium loading or exclusion can bring the risk within the range the insurer is willing to accept, or where reinsurance support is unavailable for the risk.

Under NIIRA 2025, insurers must communicate declinations in writing with a stated reason and inform the proposer of any right of review or appeal available within the company. Blanket declinations based solely on HIV/AIDS status are prohibited (see Section 11.7.3). Declined proposers may be referred to specialist insurers or impaired life markets where available.

A simplified underwriting approach used primarily in group and bancassurance business in which the insurer accepts all members of the group or all qualifying borrowers as insured without individual medical evidence, subject to the application of a moratorium: a defined period (typically 12–24 months) during which claims arising from pre-existing conditions are excluded. The moratorium converts individual medical underwriting into a time-based exclusion that applies uniformly across the group.

Moratorium underwriting is widely used in the Nigerian market for group life schemes (particularly employer-sponsored schemes where universal coverage is a requirement), for credit life products embedded in bank loans, and for group health riders. Its advantages are: elimination of the administrative burden of individual medical evidence collection; faster scheme implementation; and inclusion of members who might otherwise be declined or heavily loaded on an individual basis.

The underwriting risk under a moratorium scheme is that claims arising from pre-existing conditions in the moratorium period are declined. The insurer must therefore ensure that: the moratorium clause is clearly disclosed in the master policy and member certificates; the insurer can reliably identify and substantiate pre-existing condition claims; and the claims handling team applies the moratorium consistently and fairly. NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions require that moratorium exclusions be disclosed in policyholder documentation in plain language.

Occupational hazard classification is the systematic ranking of occupations by the degree of excess mortality risk they present relative to the standard population assumption used in life assurance pricing. Most life insurers in Nigeria use a four- or five-class system derived from reinsurer occupational hazard schedules, adapted for the Nigerian labour market.

rows: Light office or professional work; no physical hazard. Standard rates apply without occupational loading.
Accountants, civil servants, lawyers, teachers, doctors in clinical practice, office administrators, bankers, retail managers.
Some physical activity or minor hazard; low elevation above standard mortality. Standard rates or minor loading.
Drivers (personal vehicles, cars), pharmacists, veterinarians, laboratory technicians, light industrial supervisors.
Regular physical risk or elevated exposure to accident or disease. Loading required (typically 50–150% of standard premium or a flat extra).
Heavy goods vehicle drivers, construction site workers, electricians (industrial), miners (surface), agricultural workers, police officers (non-combat), firemen.
Significant, ongoing physical hazard with materially elevated accident/death risk. Heavy loading or exclusion required.
Offshore oil and gas workers, deep-sea fishermen, military personnel (active duty), armed security personnel, explosives handlers, miners (underground).
Hazard so extreme that standard life insurance is not available, or only available with severe restrictions and reinsurer support.
Combat soldiers in active conflict zones, certain specialist paramilitary roles. Typically declined or referred to specialist markets.

blocks.h: The occupational classification schedule must be maintained as a live document. The Nigerian labour market includes a large informal sector where occupational descriptions are imprecise. An underwriter who receives a proposal from a ‘businessman’ must probe the nature of the business: a transport business owner who personally drives inter-state routes carries a Class 3 or 4 risk; the same individual who manages the business administratively without driving is a Class 1 or 2 risk.

Reinsurers are a critical source of occupational hazard data and underwriting guidance. Most reinsurance treaties include an occupational hazard schedule as an exhibit, and reinsurers will typically provide additional guidance on unusual occupational descriptions on request.

Aviation risk in life assurance underwriting is categorised as passenger aviation risk (commercial airline passengers) and private aviation risk (private pilots and passengers in non-commercial aviation).

Commercial airline passengers: Regular international air travel on scheduled commercial airlines is treated as a standard risk in contemporary life underwriting. The per-mile mortality rate on international scheduled flights is lower than that for private motor vehicle travel. No loading applies for commercial air travel frequency.

Private aviation: Private piloting carries materially elevated mortality risk relative to commercial aviation. The mortality rate for private pilots is significantly higher than for non-pilots of the same age, primarily due to the inherent instability of light aircraft, weather exposure, and the lower mandatory training standards compared to commercial aviation. Most Nigerian life insurers apply either a flat extra premium (typically ₦2.50–₦5.00 per ₦1,000 sum assured) for licensed private pilots, or an exclusion of claims arising from private aviation activities.

Key information required for aviation underwriting: pilot’s licence type; current medical fitness certificate; total flying hours; types of aircraft flown; extent of instrument flying; any history of accidents or near-misses; whether flying is purely recreational or for business purposes.

Drug use and substance abuse present complex underwriting challenges because they elevate mortality risk through multiple pathways: the direct toxic effects of the substance; the elevated risk of accidental death (road accidents, falls, drowning, overdose); the associated lifestyle risks (HIV transmission through needle sharing; violence associated with drug procurement); and the underlying psychological or social conditions that often accompany addiction.
Underwriting responses to drug use in Nigerian life practice follow a graduated approach:

items.h: Casual or experimental past use (no current use; no evidence of dependency or associated illness): standard or light loading depending on substance and duration.

Past dependency, now in recovery (verified period of abstinence, clinical support): postponement until minimum recovery period (typically 24–48 months drug-free); loading or exclusion on reapplication.
Current use of any illegal narcotic substance: postpone or decline depending on severity, substance, and evidence of associated complications.
IV drug use, past or present: significant loading or declination due to HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C transmission risk. HIV serology and liver function tests required.

blocks.h: The proposal form should ask clear, specific questions about drug use history. Some Nigerian proposers may not disclose drug use in a written declaration but may do so in a tele-underwriting interview. Insurers that have implemented tele-underwriting channels report higher disclosure rates on sensitive questions compared to paper forms.

HIV/AIDS underwriting has undergone a fundamental transformation globally over the past two decades, driven by the dramatic improvement in clinical outcomes for HIV-positive individuals on modern antiretroviral therapy (ART). A person diagnosed with HIV today, commenced on ART within the first year of infection and maintaining an undetectable viral load, has a life expectancy close to that of an HIV-negative person of the same age. This change in the clinical landscape has made wholesale declination of HIV-positive applicants both actuarially unjustified and, in many jurisdictions, legally impermissible.

In Nigeria, NIIRA 2025 imposes a specific non-discrimination obligation: no insurer may decline a life assurance application solely on the basis of the applicant’s HIV-positive status. The insurer must conduct an individualised assessment of the applicant’s current clinical status. This obligation aligns with the National HIV/AIDS Anti-Discrimination Policy of the Federal Government of Nigeria and reflects the scale of Nigeria’s HIV burden, with approximately 1.7 million Nigerians living with HIV, a blanket exclusionary policy would represent a significant market conduct failure.

blocks.title: Advisory: HIV/AIDS Underwriting: Individualised Assessment Framework

blocks.h: Under NIIRA 2025, the following assessment framework is required for HIV-positive applicants:

items.h: Clinical evidence required: Applicant must provide (a) a current CD4 count (minimum threshold typically 350 cells/μL for standard consideration); (b) HIV viral load (undetectable preferred; detectable but suppressed may attract loading); (c) duration on ART; (d) ART regimen and compliance history; (e) evidence of absence of AIDS-defining illnesses.

Underwriting outcome by clinical status: (i) CD4 > 500, undetectable viral load, on stable ART > 2 years: loading 100–150% of standard premium; (ii) CD4 350–500, suppressed viral load: loading 150–250%; (iii) CD4 < 350 or detectable viral load: postpone; reapply when clinical status improves.

Benefit limitations: For HIV-positive applicants, pure risk covers (term assurance, group life) are the primary product. Savings-linked or participating policies present additional reserving complexity due to longer duration; individual insurer policy and reinsurer support govern availability.

Data protection: HIV status is sensitive personal health data under the NDPA 2023. Collection, storage, use, and disclosure are subject to strict data minimisation and security requirements. HIV test results may not be shared beyond the underwriting function without the applicant’s explicit consent.

blocks.h: Financial underwriting is the process of assessing whether the sum assured proposed is financially justifiable relative to the applicant’s verifiable economic interest in their own life (for personal policies) or in the life of the insured (for third-party policies). Its purpose is to ensure that the insurance is written to replace an economic loss, not to generate a financial gain, and to prevent the moral hazard that arises when insurance creates a financial incentive for harm.

Financial underwriting also serves as the first line of defence against the use of life insurance as a money laundering vehicle. Large single-premium policies, policies taken out and surrendered shortly after issue for cash value, and proposals funded from opaque sources are all potential indicators of financial crime that the underwriting function is positioned to detect.

Insurable interest is the legal requirement that the proposer must have a recognised economic or relationship-based interest in the life being insured at the time the policy is taken out. Without insurable interest, the policy is a wagering contract and is void. In Nigerian law (rooted in the Life Assurance Act 1774 as received and in the Insurance Act 2003 as superseded by NIIRA 2025), insurable interest exists in the following relationships:

items.h: A person has an unlimited insurable interest in their own life.
A spouse has an insurable interest in the life of their spouse (and vice versa), subject to proof of marriage.
A creditor has an insurable interest in the life of a debtor to the extent of the outstanding debt; this is the foundation of credit life insurance.
An employer has an insurable interest in the life of a key employee to the extent of the financial loss the employer would suffer from the employee’s death, the basis of keyman insurance.
Business partners have insurable interests in each other’s lives to the extent of their respective business interests, the basis of partnership protection policies.

blocks.h: Where insurable interest is not clearly established, the underwriter must request supporting documentation before proceeding: marriage certificate, loan agreement, employment contract, or business ownership evidence as appropriate.

blocks.text: 11.8.3 Income Multiples and Sum Assured Limits

blocks.h: For personal life assurance, the standard financial underwriting tool is the income multiple: the maximum sum assured that will be considered relative to the proposer’s annual income. Income multiples are set to reflect the economic replacement cost of the proposer’s income over their remaining working life, discounted to present value, a calculation that declines as the proposer approaches retirement.

rows: Up to 5 times (or to retirement age based on discounted earnings)

blocks.h: Source: Indicative of Nigerian market practice aligned with reinsurer guidelines. Individual insurers may use different multiples based on their product design and reinsurance treaty terms.

blocks.text: 11.8.4 AML/CFT Obligations in the Underwriting Process

blocks.h: Life insurance is classified as a financial product with money laundering exposure under Nigeria’s Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022 (MLPPA 2022) and the relevant NAICOM anti-money laundering guidelines. Life insurers are required to implement a Know Your Customer (KYC) programme that is applied consistently to all applicants at the point of underwriting.
KYC obligations at underwriting include:

items.h: Identity verification: National Identity Number (NIN), government-issued photo ID, BVN for premium payment accounts.
Source of funds: For single-premium policies or large regular-premium policies, evidence of the source of funds used to pay premiums (payslips, business accounts, investment statements).
Beneficial ownership: For corporate or trust-held policies, identification of the ultimate beneficial owner.
Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) screening: All proposers must be screened against PEP lists. PEP proposals require enhanced due diligence and senior management approval before acceptance.
Sanctions screening: Screening against UN, OFAC, and domestic sanctions lists.

blocks.h: Red flags that should trigger additional AML investigation during underwriting: a premium amount inconsistent with the proposer’s stated income; request for a single-premium policy funded by a cash payment or from an untraceable source; a proposal for a very large sum assured by a young proposer with limited declared income and no clear financial need; a proposer who is uncooperative with KYC documentation requests; and a beneficiary who has no apparent insurable interest in the life assured.

blocks.title: Suspicious Transaction Indicators in Life Assurance Underwriting

blocks.h: Underwriters should escalate to the Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) where any of the following indicators are present:

items.h: Proposer insists on paying a large single premium by cash, third-party transfer, or cryptocurrency.
The proposed sum assured is significantly in excess of the income multiples applicable to the declared income, with no satisfactory explanation.
Proposer is unwilling to provide standard KYC documentation or provides documentation that appears inconsistent or forged.
Policy is proposed by a person with no established residency or income history in Nigeria on behalf of a non-resident beneficiary.
Proposer has multiple existing policies with several insurers aggregating to a sum assured far in excess of any plausible financial need.
Policy is taken out and a request to surrender for cash value is made within a short period of issue (early surrender requests are a classic structuring indicator).

blocks.text: 11.9 NIIRA 2025 and Actuarial Oversight of Underwriting

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 introduces a framework of actuarial oversight that extends explicitly to underwriting practices. The statutory actuary is required to confirm, in the annual actuarial report submitted to NAICOM, that the company’s underwriting practices are consistent with its pricing bases and that the risk selection framework does not, in the statutory actuary’s opinion, expose the company to material adverse deviation from its pricing assumptions.
This places a direct professional duty on the statutory actuary in relation to underwriting governance. In practice, this means the statutory actuary must:

items.h: Review the company’s NMLs annually and confirm they are consistent with current reinsurance treaty requirements and current claims experience.

Review the actuarial consistency of occupational hazard loadings and medical underwriting guidelines, and flag where the guidelines are not supported by the company’s claims data or by published actuarial evidence.
Review the terms of all reinsurance treaties (automatic and facultative) and confirm that the treaty bases are consistent with the pricing bases used for NAICOM product filings.
Review aggregated underwriting data to identify systematic patterns of anti-selection that are not being detected by the current underwriting process.
Report to the Board and NAICOM on any material deficiency in the underwriting control framework.

blocks.h: NAICOM’s powers under NIIRA 2025 also include the authority to direct an insurer to revise its underwriting guidelines where NAICOM’s own review suggests that the guidelines are inappropriate, inconsistent, or materially deficient. This power was relatively rarely exercised under the Insurance Act 2003; NIIRA 2025’s broader supervisory remit and the strengthened NAICOM enforcement capacity makes active regulatory engagement with underwriting governance more likely.

Reinsurance is the mechanism by which a direct insurer (the cedant) transfers a portion of its underwriting risk to a reinsurer in exchange for a proportionate share of the premium. In the context of individual life underwriting, reinsurance serves two distinct functions: it provides capacity for large sums assured that exceed the insurer’s own retention limit, and it provides underwriting expertise and guidance for complex or unusual risks.

Under an automatic (treaty) reinsurance arrangement, every policy that falls within the terms of the treaty is automatically reinsured to the agreed proportion without the need for individual case referral. The most common treaty structure in Nigerian life reinsurance is the Yearly Renewable Term (YRT) treaty, under which the reinsurer provides excess-of-retention life cover each year, renewable on the anniversary of the policy.

The retention limit is the maximum net amount at risk (the death benefit less any policy reserve) that the direct insurer retains for its own account on any single life. Amounts above the retention limit are ceded to the reinsurer under the treaty. For a Nigerian life insurer with a retention limit of ₦50 million, a policy with a sum assured of ₦150 million would result in ₦50 million retained and ₦100 million ceded.

The treaty also specifies the automatic binding limit; the maximum sum assured the reinsurer will automatically accept under the treaty without individual case review. Amounts above the automatic binding limit require facultative referral (see Section 11.10.2).

Facultative reinsurance involves the referral of an individual risk to one or more reinsurers for individual underwriting assessment. The reinsurer is free to accept, decline, or offer modified terms on the facultative submission. Facultative referral is used where:

items.h: The proposed sum assured exceeds the treaty’s automatic binding limit.
The risk involves a medical impairment, occupational hazard, or combination of factors outside the automatic treaty’s underwriting guidelines.
The direct insurer wants reinsurer underwriting support on an unusual or complex case before committing to a decision.

The treaty specifically excludes the risk category (e.g., some treaties exclude HIV-positive applicants; this is now in tension with NIIRA 2025’s non-discrimination obligation, requiring treaty renegotiation).

blocks.h: A facultative submission to the reinsurer includes: the completed proposal form and all medical evidence collected; the underwriter’s own preliminary assessment of the risk; a cover note specifying the sum assured requested and the cedant’s proposed retention; and any other material information bearing on the risk. The reinsurer typically responds within 5 to 15 business days with a facultative quotation specifying the terms on which they will accept the risk.

Where a facultative quotation is received, the direct insurer must decide whether to: accept the reinsurer’s terms and issue the policy on that basis; accept the risk on its own account at reduced sum assured; or decline the proposal. The reinsurer’s opinion is advisory to the direct insurer: the direct insurer retains the contractual relationship with the policyholder and remains liable for the full sum assured regardless of whether the reinsurer meets its obligations under the treaty.

Beyond individual facultative referrals, reinsurers provide a range of underwriting support services to their cedant insurers in Nigeria. These include: underwriting manual development and periodic revision; occupational hazard schedule maintenance; claims data analysis and feedback on underwriting adequacy; training for underwriting staff; medical director consultations for complex medical cases; and mortality experience analysis services. Access to reinsurer expertise is particularly valuable in the Nigerian market where the insurer’s own claims experience base may be insufficient to develop independent underwriting assumptions.

blocks.text: 11.11 Advisory: Underwriting Best Practices for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: This section addresses the operational design of a high-performing underwriting function in the Nigerian market. It is directed at Chief Underwriting Officers, actuarial leaders, and senior product managers responsible for the ongoing governance of the underwriting framework.

blocks.text: 11.11.1 Triage Models: Accelerated, Simplified, and Full Underwriting

blocks.h: A triage model categorises incoming applications by risk profile at the point of receipt and routes each application to the appropriate underwriting track. The objective is to apply medical evidence collection and detailed underwriting assessment proportionately, only to the cases that require it, while clearing low-risk cases quickly at low cost. A well-designed triage model can achieve Straight-Through Processing (STP) rates of 60–80% for clean applications in a digital channel.

rows: Young age band (under 40); sum assured below NML; all health declarations negative; clean financial underwriting; no occupational hazard flag.
Automated decision engine; policy issued without human underwriter review.
Age 40–55 below NML with clear declarations; or any age with minor occupational hazard; or sum assured slightly above NML with clean health declarations.
Human underwriter review; no medical examination required; decision based on declarations and financial check.
Any case exceeding NML; any non-trivial health disclosure; age 55+ for significant sums assured; complex occupational hazard; AML flag.
Full medical evidence collection; Attending Physician Statement or specialist report as required; reinsurer referral if needed.
10–21 business days (dependent on medical evidence turnaround).

blocks.h: The traditional medical evidence pipeline in Nigerian life underwriting (paper proposal forms, physical GP examinations, hand-carried APS reports) is a material bottleneck. Average new business turnaround times in the Nigerian market have historically exceeded 15–25 business days for cases requiring medical evidence, compared to 5–10 days in more digitally advanced markets. This turnaround gap has commercial consequences: it drives lapse-before-issue (applications abandoned before the policy is issued) and creates competitive disadvantage against distribution channels that do not require medical evidence (group schemes, microinsurance, simple credit life).
Best-practice initiatives for digital evidence gathering include:

items.h: Tele-underwriting: Trained interviewers conduct structured health disclosure calls with applicants, replacing or supplementing the paper proposal form health section. Nigerian insurers that have implemented tele-underwriting report 15–25% improvement in medical disclosure completeness and a reduction in post-claim non-disclosure disputes.

Digital medical examiner reporting: Medical examiners complete examination forms on a dedicated portal, eliminating paper transcription delays and enabling automatic flagging of out-of-range results. Real-time examination result feeds into the underwriting system reduce turnaround time for cases requiring examination by 3–5 business days.

eHealth record integration: Where available and with appropriate consent, integration with electronic patient records (from private hospital networks) can supplement or replace the APS. This is an emerging capability in the Nigerian market; current coverage is limited to a small number of private health providers in Lagos and Abuja.

Wearable and biometric data: A small number of Nigerian insurers are piloting programmes under which applicants who provide consent to share fitness tracker or health monitoring data receive simplified underwriting treatment or premium discounts. This is currently a product innovation initiative rather than a mainstream underwriting tool.

blocks.h: Underwriting turnaround time (TAT) is a key operational metric with direct commercial impact. Applications that remain in the underwriting queue represent unissued premiums, uncommissioned agents, and potentially lost customers. Insurers that track and manage TAT as a first-class KPI consistently outperform those that treat it as an administrative by-product.
Recommended KPIs for the Nigerian life underwriting function:

rows: Percentage of applications issued at standard terms without human underwriter intervention. Target: 60%+ for digital channels; 40%+ for paper/agent channels.
Time from complete application receipt to policy issue for STP cases. Target: < 24 hours (digital); < 3 business days (paper).
Time from complete application to decision for simplified underwriting cases. Target: < 3 business days.
Time from receipt of last required medical evidence to final underwriting decision. Target: < 5 business days.
Time from medical evidence request to receipt of completed evidence. Target: < 10 business days (GP examination); < 15 business days (APS).
Percentage of applications received that are not ultimately converted to in-force policies, due to delays or abandonment. Target: < 5% for individual business.
Percentage of applications declined. Used to monitor for systematic anti-selection in distribution channels or geographic segments. Benchmark against reinsurer norms.
Percentage of death claims where the insurer disputes coverage on grounds of non-disclosure. A high rate may indicate inadequate proposal form disclosure capture or tele-underwriting quality issues.

blocks.h: Inconsistency in underwriting decisions (where two underwriters with the same evidence reach materially different conclusions about the same risk) is a source of both financial and reputational risk. It creates potential claims disputes where declined or loaded applicants challenge the decision by reference to earlier approvals for similar risks. It exposes the insurer to regulatory scrutiny under NIIRA 2025’s market conduct provisions. And it creates a persistency problem: if agents learn that persistent escalation or channel switching produces different underwriting outcomes, they develop workarounds that systematically undermine risk selection.
Consistency frameworks include:

items.h: Underwriting manual standardisation: A comprehensive, regularly updated underwriting manual that specifies the decision criteria, loadings, and special terms applicable to all common impairments and risk factors. The manual should be the single authoritative source for underwriting decisions; it should not be possible for an underwriter to justify a decision that departs from the manual without escalating to the Chief Underwriting Officer.

Peer review and quality assurance: A structured programme of peer review of underwriting decisions, including regular audit of samples of issued policies (standard and non-standard), declined applications, and reinsurer referrals. Quality assurance findings should feed back into underwriter performance management and manual revision.

Decision override tracking: All decisions that depart from the underwriting manual must be documented, with stated reasons, and logged in a central register. Patterns of upward override (approvals of cases the manual would decline) should be reviewed by the statutory actuary as part of underwriting adequacy oversight.

Reinsurer agreement: Regular (annual or biennial) underwriting audit by the treaty reinsurer, who will review a sample of the insurer’s underwriting decisions against the treaty’s underwriting basis. Reinsurer audit findings are a valuable independent quality check.

blocks.h: The underwriting function’s effectiveness is ultimately determined by the competence of the underwriters who exercise judgment on individual cases. In Nigeria, formal underwriting training pathways are underdeveloped compared to more mature insurance markets. Most underwriters learn primarily on the job, supplemented by reinsurer training programmes. Building a structured competency framework is a strategic investment in underwriting quality.
A recommended competency framework for Nigerian life underwriters comprises five domains:

rows: Human anatomy and physiology; pathology of common impairments; interpretation of clinical test results; pharmacology of common treatments.
Reinsurer-provided medical underwriting courses (Munich Re, Swiss Re, Africa Re); CIIN Medical Underwriting module; annual medical update sessions with clinical advisors.
Mortality tables and qx; premium calculation mechanics; the relationship between loading methodology and pricing assumptions; profitability impact of underwriting decisions.
CIIN examination curriculum (Actuarial Concepts: Chapter 13); statutory actuary workshops; actuarial team presentations.
NIIRA 2025 consumer protection obligations; non-disclosure law; insurable interest; AML/CFT; HIV non-discrimination; NDPA 2023 data obligations.
CIIN professional development; NAICOM industry circulars; in-house legal and compliance training.
Risk classification; weighing of multiple impairments; special terms application; triage decision-making; reinsurer communication.
Supervised caseload with graduated case complexity; peer review participation; facultative referral participation.
Income multiples; insurable interest verification; AML red flag identification; PEP screening.
CIIN AML module; NAICOM AML guidelines training; in-house financial crime awareness.

blocks.h: The process by which a life insurer assesses an individual applicant’s risk profile and determines whether to accept the risk for insurance and, if so, on what terms and at what premium rate.

The tendency for individuals with higher-than-average mortality risk to disproportionately seek insurance, or to seek larger amounts of it, relative to low-risk individuals. Underwriting is the primary mechanism for managing anti-selection.
The maximum sum assured up to which a life insurer will issue a policy based solely on the applicant’s health declarations, without requiring a medical examination.
A simplified group underwriting approach under which individual medical evidence is waived, but claims arising from pre-existing conditions within a defined moratorium period are excluded.
A fixed additional annual premium per ₦1,000 sum assured applied to an impaired risk, regardless of the applicant’s age. Appropriate for impairments with approximately constant excess mortality.

A multiplicative increase in the standard premium applied to an impaired risk (e.g., 150% of standard premium). Appropriate for impairments with excess mortality proportionate to baseline age-specific mortality.

A structured report completed by the applicant’s treating doctor at the insurer’s request, providing clinical detail on a disclosed condition. The most informative third-party medical evidence tool in life underwriting.
Individual-case reinsurance in which the cedant refers a specific risk to the reinsurer for separate underwriting assessment and pricing, outside the automatic treaty framework.
The maximum net amount at risk (death benefit less reserve) that the direct insurer retains on any single life for its own account. Amounts above this limit are ceded to the reinsurer.
The assessment of whether the proposed sum assured is financially justified by the applicant’s economic interest. Prevents over-insurance and moral hazard; also the first line of AML defence.
The legal requirement that the proposer must have a recognised economic or relationship-based interest in the life being insured. Without insurable interest, a life policy is void.
The maximum sum assured expressed as a multiple of the applicant’s annual income. Declines with age to reflect the reducing number of remaining income-earning years.
A classification (typically Class 1 to 4) assigned to an occupation based on its physical risk relative to the standard office/professional risk assumed in the standard mortality table.
A structured health disclosure interview conducted by a trained specialist by telephone, replacing or supplementing the written health declaration section of the proposal form.
Automated policy issuance without human underwriter review, applicable to low-risk applications that satisfy all automated triage criteria.
A person who holds or has held a prominent public function. PEP proposals require enhanced due diligence under AML/CFT regulations.
